{"id": "4:6/q42", "question": "How is wa-kafā bi-llāhi ḥasīban parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the bāʾ is extra, what supplies the subject and objects, and how ḥasīban functions.", "positions": [{"id": "4:6/q42/p1", "position": "The bāʾ is extra and God is the subject of kafā", "reasons": "SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج: Al-Zajjaj says the bāʾ enters the subject because the utterance conveys a command, but the author finds this contradictory about whether bāʾ is extra and who the subject is. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author: Kafā is a verb, not a noun-like particle; its subject is the noun governed by the extra bāʾ. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء: Abu al-Baqa says the extra bāʾ signals the imperative sense ‘be content with God.’ SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya says bi-Allah is nominative after an extra preposition and that the preposition gives a statement the force of a command; the author sees this as answering al-Zajjaj by making the bāʾ extra. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عيسى: Ibn ʿIsa says bāʾ joins the phrase as both subject-like and genitive attachment, reflecting that divine sufficiency exceeds ordinary sufficiency; the author says this needs thought. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء: Abu al-Baqa treats kafā as taking two omitted objects, ‘God suffices you against them,’ citing 2:137; the author says that is a different sense and questions the analysis. | mentions 2:137 WAHIDI-BASIT (WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r7): The bāʾ is extra and God is the subject of kafā. WAHIDI-BASIT (WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r8): Hasiban may be circumstantial or specification. TABRISI (TABRISI:4:6/r3): The bāʾ is extra and God is the subject of kafā."}, {"id": "4:6/q42/p2", "position": "An implicit verbal noun can be the subject", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: The sound parse makes كفى a verb with Allah as subject and an extra ب; an alternative requires the Kufan allowance for an implicit verbal noun to govern its complement, which Basrans reject. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن السراج: Ibn al-Sarraj instead posits an implicit verbal-noun subject, ‘sufficiency,’ with bi-Allah as its semantic object; the author notes Basrans allow this only in poetic necessity. Against — SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author: The author responds that if the subject is implicit, bi-Allah need not attach to that subject; it can attach to the verb, as Makki and al-Zajjaj suggest."}, {"id": "4:6/q42/p3", "position": "Ḥasīban is an accusative of specification", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: حسيبا may be accusative as specification or circumstance; كفى can omit its object here, unlike uses where it takes two objects such as 5:48. | mentions 5:48 SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author: Ḥasīban is most likely an accusative of specification, shown by its ability to take min; the alternative is a circumstantial accusative."}, {"id": "4:6/q42/p4", "position": "Kafā has one implicit object", "reasons": "SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author: Here kafā takes one object, omitted as ‘God suffices you.’ ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السمين: Al-Samin treats kafa as taking one object, while Abu al-Baqa allows two, with the implied sense of God sparing you harm or the like."}, {"id": "4:6/q42/p5", "position": "Ḥasīban is circumstantial", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الواحدي عن الزجاج: Al-Wāḥidī transmits from al-Zajjāj that the bāʾ in wa-kafā bi-llāh and wa-kafā bi-rabbika is redundant; ḥasīban is accusative as a circumstantial expression meaning reckoning or sufficiency. | mentions 17:65"}, {"id": "4:6/q42/p6", "position": "Kafā is a verb with a divine subject", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: حسيب may be a reciprocal intensive noun or a strengthened active participle; grammarians also disagree whether كفى is a verb or a noun of action and whether its subject is Allah or an implicit مصدر."}]}
{"id": "4:6/q43", "question": "What further rhetorical choices shape this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:6/q43/p1", "position": "The wording intensifies or clarifies the command", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: A transitive act needs both an agent as influencer and an object as recipient; neither precedes the other in the act itself, so just as the agent may precede, the object may precede in wording. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: In ضرب غلامه زيد the object appears before the subject in wording, although it remains later in meaning. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: In the verse about Abraham being tested by his Lord, the subject is later in wording but earlier in meaning; making that semantic order explicit would yield an antecedent before its pronoun. | mentions 2:124 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: Witnessing protects the orphan from injustice and short delivery because the guardian cannot convincingly claim to have transferred the assets without witnesses; al-Rāzī says both the command’s wording and its purpose require it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن بن صالح بن حي: Hasan ibn Salih distinguishes the father's appointed guardian, who may take customary support, from a judge's guardian, who may take nothing. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author: Al-Qurtubi says the wording covers both repayment and any spending for a ward; witnessing is the apparent command, and a witnessed entrustment is discharged only by witnessed return. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · أبو حنيفة: Abu Hanifa sets puberty at eighteen; bulūgh al-nikāḥ euphemistically means maturity and suitability for marriage in his view. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: The apparent wording gives the guardian independent authority to hand over the estate. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: The apparent wording makes witnessing obligatory, though some say it is recommended. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: It repeats key words and meanings: fear, creation, orphan, women, inheritance, and guarding against injustice. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: The added force in فليستعفف intensifies the meaning of seeking restraint. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author: The fāʾ in ‘if you perceive’ answers idhā, and the fāʾ in ‘then hand over’ answers in. BURHAN, d. 794 · author: Expressions can differ in eloquence through the force and dignity of individual meanings and through smoothness of wording. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author: If they show sound financial judgment upon maturity, their assets must be handed over; the indefinite wording reflects how rare complete maturity is. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: The fa in give them their property signals prompt delivery at the point of entitlement; some also see a semantic distinction between paying it over here and the earlier verb give. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: The wording makes puberty the default endpoint of guardianship only when sound judgment is found, preventing guardians from keeping wards' property for their own benefit. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ثعلب: As transmitted by al-Zajjaji, Tha'lab held that the second condition in wording is first in occurrence; Ibn Malik and al-Baghawi among the Shafi'is also chose this view. Against — SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author: The author says there is no need to insert ‘the age’ or ‘the time’ of marriage: the wording means they become fit for marriage."}, {"id": "4:6/q43/p2", "position": "Attribution of the property emphasizes the orphans' entitlement", "reasons": "BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author: The pronoun shift from guardians' assets to the orphans' assets signals that property belongs to those who can manage it responsibly, ending the need for protective restriction. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: The property is attributed to the orphans because their claim becomes firmly established once mature, when their disposal no longer threatens relatives' and the community's interests."}, {"id": "4:6/q43/p3", "position": "Fronting the recipient emphasizes the orphans", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: The handover clause addresses guardians and trustees: after observing the preceding requirements, they deliver the assets under their care to the orphans; fronting the recipient emphasizes them. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Wisdom required beginning with the Prophet's own people because confronting the world's entrenched ignorance and corruption at once was not feasible; Arabic references to the audience do not make Arabs the only recipients. | mentions 14:4, 26:198, 26:199"}, {"id": "4:6/q43/p4", "position": "Handover is pictured as pushing property away from the guardian", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Ibtalā means testing; reaching the age of marriage means reaching its appropriate time, a rational metaphor for maturity. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Handing the money over is a delicate metaphor: the guardian figuratively pushes it away from himself and places it in the orphan's possession."}, {"id": "4:6/q43/p5", "position": "Ānastum calls for prompt response to the first sign", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: Choosing anistum rather than alimtum suggests that property should be handed over as soon as the first sign of sound judgment is known, without delay."}, {"id": "4:6/q43/p6", "position": "Repeated handover forms create paronomasia", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: The matching forms in “hand over” and “when you hand over” create perfect paronomasia."}]}

ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: This connection is clearer if the earlier fools are wasteful orphans; it is less clear if all orphans are called foolish based on their childhood, as another account has it. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: Another view treats the verse as a return to orphan-property rulings rather than a new beginning, on the premise that the preceding material was a digression. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: Other jurists make the final condition and its answer govern the preceding ones; some require all conditions in any order, while conjunctions alter which conditions the answer covers. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشافعي: The preferred grammatical analysis makes each later condition’s answer implicit from the preceding answer, requiring the conditions to occur in reverse nesting order; al-Jassas says Muhammad and Abu Yusuf also dispute the issue. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: The two coordinated accusatives are parsed as circumstantial accusatives, though some parse them as purpose clauses; this warning connects with the preceding prohibition, not the post-puberty conditional. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: The handover clause addresses guardians and trustees: after observing the preceding requirements, they deliver the assets under their care to the orphans; fronting the recipient emphasizes them. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The two verses organize guardianship over restricted property: how to receive, preserve, grow, use, and return it, and when to hand it over, for the public good. STUDYQURAN · Ṭ: A poor guardian may take only what necessities require, especially food; it is a loan that must be repaid even after death. | mentions 2:152, 17:34"}, {"id": "4:6/q44/p2", "position": "It specifies or reinforces 4:2's command to return orphan property", "reasons": "IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين: Nikah means the contract in 2:221, 4:3, 4:25, and 33:49. | mentions 2:221, 4:3, 4:25, 33:49 IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين: Nikah denotes both contract and intercourse in 4:22. | mentions 4:22 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: Because 4:2 ordered guardians to hand over orphan property, this verse specifies when: both puberty and discerned sound judgment must be established before delivery. | mentions 4:2 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو بكر الرازي: Abū Bakr al-Rāzī reports his school’s view that guardians may take nothing from the orphan, whether as a loan or outright and whether rich or poor; he cites 4:2, 4:10, 4:127, and 2:188 as decisive texts against the possibly ambiguous permission here. | mentions 4:2, 4:10, 4:127, 2:188 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مجاهد: Mujahid says the allowance is abrogated by the prohibition on consuming wealth without trade by mutual consent, because guardianship is not a sale. | mentions 4:29 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكيا الطبري: Al-Kiya al-Tabari agrees that the verse requires subsistence from one's own property, not the child's; he harmonizes its ambiguity with clear prohibitions on consuming another's wealth without consent, especially an orphan's. | mentions 4:29, 4:2 ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author: The meaning of fair dealing is clarified by prohibitions on consuming wealth wrongfully or unjustly, including the orphan’s property, and by the command to uphold justice for orphans. | mentions 2:188, 4:29, 4:10, 4:127 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: Alternatively, the command connects to 4:2 and explains how and when orphan property is delivered; the explicit noun is used because the antecedent is distant. | mentions 4:2 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: Permission for a poor guardian to eat customarily qualifies the general ban: a modest share supports the guardian so that earning a livelihood does not distract from managing the ward's assets. | mentions 4:2 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: The prohibition reiterates the earlier ban in 4:2 and exposes guardians who hasten to consume wards' assets before the wards mature and can demand an accounting. | mentions 4:2 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Qur'an describes enslaved women and free women as belonging to one human community and allows marriage to enslaved women with their families' consent. | mentions 4:25 Against — IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس: A minority says the permission was abrogated by 4:29, but the author says this report from Ibn ʿAbbas is unsound. | mentions 4:29 Against — RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: Al-Rāzī rejects the argument: 4:2 is general while this verse is specific, and the other prohibitions only apply if moderate guardian use is already proved unjust, which is the very issue disputed. | mentions 4:2, 4:10, 4:127, 2:188"}, {"id": "4:6/q44/p3", "position": "It completes 4:5's protection of wealth from the foolish", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: Reaching the age of marriage means puberty, identified by emission, as in 24:59; it is when legal accountability and penalties begin, and the label refers to the emission involved in intercourse. | mentions 24:59 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي: If someone first reaches sound judgment and later becomes foolish, al-Shāfiʿī would restrain him, while Abū Ḥanīfa would not; al-Rāzī supports restraint by analogy with the still-unfit minor whose property is preserved for future need. | mentions 4:5 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author: Reaching marriageable age means puberty, as shown by the Quran's parallel phrase about children reaching puberty; puberty can be established by five signs, three shared by both sexes and menstruation and pregnancy specific to women. | mentions 24:59 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author: Malik and one Shafi'i view restore guardianship if a released person becomes wasteful; Abu Hanifa says it cannot return, but al-Qurtubi cites the Quran's protection of wealth and its provision for a guardian when a debtor becomes foolish or weak. | mentions 4:5, 2:282 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: The command may connect to 4:5 as a culmination of its ban; if the earlier foolish are specifically orphans, repeating their name clarifies the rule and anticipates their hoped-for maturity. | mentions 4:5 IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: If the earlier foolish include adults generally, as the author thinks more likely, this verse singles out orphans because puberty is a foreseeable time for change; adult folly has no predictable testing point. | mentions 4:5 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Good speech is the ethical basis for dealing with the vulnerable, and monotheistic accountability supplies the foundation and lasting force of the rules. | mentions 4:5, 4:6 Against — QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو الفرج الجوزي: Al-Jawzi answers that God dignified wealth as human sustenance, prohibited entrusting it to the foolish, and ordered its return when orphans attain sound judgment. | mentions 4:5, 4:6"}, {"id": "4:6/q44/p4", "position": "It prepares the following inheritance rules", "reasons": "ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author: The discussion now moves on to inheritance rulings."}]}
{"id": "4:6/q45", "question": "What inward readings are given for this verse?", "turns_on": "How the orphan, wealth, and handover are applied to spiritual discipleship.", "positions": [{"id": "4:6/q45/p1", "position": "Testing and handover symbolize preparing disciples for guidance", "reasons": "SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ: The Shaykh rejects the hidden verbal-noun analysis because it leaves an omitted subject and makes an omitted noun govern its complement. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ: The Shaykh explains that grammarians agree idhā usually carries conditional meaning; denials mean only that it does not govern jussive verbs. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشافعي: Al-Shafiʿi and the two Hanafi disciples follow the verse’s apparent requirement that property is withheld if puberty arrives without financial maturity. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: Perfect shaykhs are charged to appoint successors and authorize disciples who are fit to guide others. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: Testing the orphans signifies testing deficient wayfarers; reaching marriage means becoming ready for guidance, and sound judgment means steadiness on the path without fickleness. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The report is an inner application: the Imams are believers' fathers, believers are orphans of knowledge when separated from them, and love qualifies them to receive higher instruction in their inherited true knowledge. | mentions 4:6"}, {"id": "4:6/q45/p2", "position": "Spiritual guides must not consume disciples' gifts", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · شيخ الإسلام: Shaykh al-Islam says the command begins specifying when and on what condition orphan wealth is returned, following the general order to give it and the ban on entrusting it to fools. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: Not consuming the disciples' wealth means not benefiting from their spiritual gifts to their exclusion or rushing before they mature into guidance; this is a grave disease of the ego. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: A spiritually rich guardian should abstain from a disciple's resources; one unable to bear need may benefit only to necessity's measure. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: Handing over the wealth means entrusting spiritual secrets only to free and worthy people."}, {"id": "4:6/q45/p3", "position": "Rushd inwardly means love of the Prophet's family", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · جعفر بن محمد عليه السلام: An esoteric report reads sound judgment as love for the family of Muhammad and says to raise such people a degree. | mentions 4:6"}, {"id": "4:6/q45/p4", "position": "The spiritual handover calls for a covenant witnessed by God", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: A spiritual handover calls for witnessing God and the spirits of the divine presence and takin

{"id": "4:6/q46", "question": "What broader historical or interpretive context is supplied?", "turns_on": "Which broader social, legal, or rhetorical setting the source is discussing.", "positions": [{"id": "4:6/q46/p1", "position": "The source supplies a related legal or ethical context", "reasons": "QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet told Hind to take enough customary support for herself and her child; another report about a son asking to be fed indicates this applies to one unable to earn. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عطاء والزهري: Ata, al-Zuhri, and Kufan jurists say a wife cannot seek separation for her husband's poverty and should await payment as a court debt; they cite the respite for an insolvent debtor and the encouragement to marry the poor. | mentions 2:280, 24:32 IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أبو عبيد: Abu Ubayd explains ibtihār as falsely claiming sex, while ibtiyār means the claim is true; al-Kumayt's verse witnesses the distinction between the two words. BURSEVI, d. 1127 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet warns that a wronged person must be appeased before the Hereafter, when good deeds are transferred or the victim’s sins are imposed. BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author: One who has repented from many wrongs but cannot find the victims should increase good deeds and keep some acts sincerely private, hoping for divine reconciliation. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: God is true existence and sees hidden betrayals and inward secrets; He is the sufficient protector."}, {"id": "4:6/q46/p2", "position": "The broader social history explains the law", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Among the early family supporters were Khadija, Hamza, Ubayd, and Abu Talib; Shi'i reports and poems attest Abu Talib's faith, which he concealed to protect the Prophet. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The Prophet is instructed to invite people with wisdom, good admonition, and the best argument. | mentions 18:110, 15:88, 41:34, 74:6, 16:125 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Pre-Islamic Arabs lived amid Christian, Zoroastrian, Jewish, and polytheist neighbors, while most were themselves tribal polytheists; this produced a crude mixture of customs. | mentions 6:116 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Poverty led fathers to kill children for fear of destitution and bury daughters; men regarded birth of a girl as distressing. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The Prophet included the call to worship one God and not lord over one another in a letter to Heraclius; the author says it was reportedly sent to other rulers too. | mentions 3:64 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The Qur'an's statement that people are created as peoples and tribes and honored by piety counters inherited status distinctions. | mentions 49:13 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Islam's call confronts entrenched corruption by installing truth, purifying belief and conduct, and completing divine grace without imposing hardship. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The Prophet and his purified family exemplified this uncompromising commitment to truth. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Moving from general principles to details is pedagogical accommodation and care for public welfare, not compromise or laxity. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The Qur'an calls the pre-Islamic Arab era ignorance because ignorance and falsehood, not knowledge and truth, governed its life. | mentions 3:154, 5:50, 48:26, 33:33 Against — TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: He condemns church inquisitions for punishing alleged religious deviation, including scientific opinions, and says church-led Crusades devastated lands and killed millions. Against — TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Political expediency might win allies to reform others, but using forbidden means cannot produce a true end; means shape the result."}, {"id": "4:6/q46/p3", "position": "Revelation and social reform unfold gradually", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The third dimension of gradual guidance has three levels: verbal invitation, religious separation from unbelief and its practices, and armed struggle. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Changing entrenched practices is harder than changing beliefs because people have longer familiarity with action; therefore beliefs came generally first and laws were disclosed in stages. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Islam's comprehensive reach across human life could not ordinarily be imposed all at once, so revelation moved from general principles to detailed rulings. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Early Meccan revelations conveyed monotheism, resurrection, piety, and worship in broad outline before later detailed legislation. | mentions 96:6, 96:14, 74:1, 74:3, 91:7, 91:10, 87:14, 87:15, 41:6, 41:8 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Gradual teaching continued in Medina; not all religious laws were revealed at once, and the staged treatment of wine illustrates the method. | mentions 16:67, 6:151, 2:219, 5:90, 5:91 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The prohibition of wine unfolded in stages: Qur'an 16:67 hints that intoxication is not good provision, 6:151 forbids sin without naming wine, 2:219 identifies its sin, and 5:90–91 completes prohibition. | mentions 16:67, 6:151, 2:219, 5:90, 5:91 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Staged disclosure in these and similar cases eases implementation and acceptance; the Qur'an was sent down over time for measured recitation. | mentions 17:106, 16:44 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Had the entire Qur'an and its detailed law been delivered together, people could not have understood, borne, accepted, or lived under it; gradual revelation made acceptance possible. | mentions 16:44 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The staged revelation also gently strengthened the Prophet, as indicated by the disbelievers' request for one complete revelation and the answer that it was arranged in measured recitation. | mentions 25:32"}, {"id": "4:6/q46/p4", "position": "Recitation length is taught through oral practice", "reasons": "NASHR, d. 833 · author: Length distinctions form a gradual scale from the shortest to the longest; the measurable element is the increment itself, learned through oral practice, imitation, and testing. NASHR, d. 833 · أبو عمرو الداني: Al-Dani says reciters' differences follow their habits in articulation and reading speed; none exceeds ordinary Arabic or accepted recitation, and direct teaching clarifies the practice. NASHR, d. 833 · author: Teachers may deliberately overtrain a student in precision, length, and articulation so the student lands on the permitted amount. NASHR, d. 833 · حمزة: Hamza says he lengthens for a young student so the student reaches the intended meaning; the author explains this as correcting underperformance. NASHR, d. 833 · حمزة: Hamza warns against excess: beyond the natural limit is not recitation. The author says this second case corrects overperformance; Hamza also calls emphatic practice training for students. NASHR, d. 833 · حمزة: When al-Thawri asked about Hamza's hamza, separation, and emphasis, Hamza answered that it was practice for the learner."}, {"id": "4:6/q46/p5", "position": "The prelude reforms family, property, and orphan practices", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Jewish and Christian societies were stratified under arbitrary rulers who seized people's lives, honor, and property; religious authorities helped govern doctrine and daily life. TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Class hierarchy extended to wealth, slavery, and gender, leaving women and children subordinate; Qur'an's call that none become another's lord captures the issue. | mentions 3:64 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: God does not waste the work of either sex; men and women are mutually of one another. | mentions 3:195 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: Inheritance was likewise prepared for gradually: the Prophet first paired companions as brothers and made them inherit one another, before kin became more entitled to inherit. | mentions 33:6 TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The opening prelude prepares for inheritance and marriage laws, two major legal structures that shape population, wealth, and society's survival."}, {"id": "4:6/q46/p6", "position": "Grammatical examples explain subject, object, and ellipsis", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author: The ordinary analysis makes the pronoun in ربه refer to an earlier mention; Ibn Jinnī allows it to refer to ʿAdī, contrary to the majority, but Razi says the argument should be framed differently. {"id": "40:55/q05", "question": "What does God's promise encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether the promise is limited to worldly aid, extends to reward after death, or includes all divine promises.", "positions": [{"id": "40:55/q05/p1", "position": "God will support Muhammad, the believers and their message, vindicating them against opponents in this world.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says the promise gives victory over deniers; Wāḥidī and Baghawī include destruction of enemies.
